title: Dimensional Modeling - Microsoft Fabric
summary: Microsoft's entry point into a dimensional-modeling series for Fabric Warehouse, framing star schema (fact + dimension tables) as the recommended design approach for a Fabric data warehouse and as a prerequisite for well-performing enterprise Power BI semantic models.
audience: Data warehouse designers and BI developers building a Fabric Warehouse who need the conceptual grounding before working through the series' fact-table, dimension-table, and load-table articles.
why_it_matters: It positions dimensional modeling as a deliberate, planned undertaking rather than an incidental byproduct of ETL, and draws the line between a governed warehouse-based model and a lighter Power-Query-only semantic model, which affects whether historical change tracking is even possible.
takeaways: Star schema is Microsoft's recommended default design for a Fabric Warehouse, not just one option among many.
The choice between a warehouse-backed dimensional model and a Power-Query-only semantic model is really a choice about whether you need historical change tracking.
A star schema's low-maintenance evolution (adding columns/facts/dimensions) is called out as a structural benefit, not just a performance one.
Data warehouses should be built out iteratively by subject area rather than attempted as one big-bang project.

claims.text: Microsoft recommends star schema (fact and dimension tables) as the design approach for building a Fabric Warehouse.

In a star schema, dimension tables describe business entities (products, people, places, dates) while fact tables store measurable events (sales orders, stock balances, exchange rates) along with the dimension keys needed to relate them.

A star schema is named for its shape: one fact table sits at the center with related dimension tables radiating outward like points of a star, and a warehouse commonly contains multiple fact tables forming multiple stars.
A well-designed star schema improves relational query performance because it needs fewer table joins and benefits more from useful indexes.
Star schema design keeps ongoing warehouse maintenance low because adding a new dimension attribute or a new fact/dimension as scope grows is a relatively simple structural change.
A dimensional model built in a Fabric Warehouse is the recommended prerequisite for an enterprise-grade Power BI semantic model, and it also serves as a data source for machine learning models.
Self-service analysts can instead build a quasi-dimensional model directly in a semantic model using Power Query to connect to and transform source data, skipping a warehouse-based ETL layer.

Defining a dimensional model purely through Power Query in the semantic model forfeits the ability to manage historical change in dimensions; a data warehouse with periodic ETL is required if accurate historical analysis is a requirement.

A data warehouse should be treated as a core, foundational component of an organization's data platform, aiming to be a single version of the truth with fast performance, understandable data, and permission enforcement.

Microsoft recommends building an enterprise data warehouse iteratively, starting with the highest-priority subject areas and extending it over time rather than attempting to design the whole warehouse at once.
Periodically (for example daily), an ETL process synchronizes dimensional model tables in the warehouse with source operational systems to keep the model current.
